answer_text:
You are not failing. Among us, wanting to believe and not yet believing was where many began. We had no word for what you call a 'crisis of faith' - and we would not have asked you to force belief. What we held was this: faith is a foundation, not a finish line. It is something to stand on while the rest is still dark. Our teacher Clement insisted that faith was the starting floor, not the ceiling. The believer is meant to grow from faith into understanding, and growing means asking.

So we would not have shut the door. We would have said: stay, and keep asking. We asked people to stay near - to listen, to ask questions, to walk with a teacher, sometimes for years, before ever coming to the water.. We cannot make it happen for you either, and we will not pretend we can. But we can tell you what we would have done: we would have walked the road with you.

And here is what we would not have done: we would not have treated your doubt as sin. Doubt aimed at understanding was hunger, not failure. Our teachers built their whole method on questions. What the apostles delivered plainly stayed fixed. Everything else was open ground, and walking that ground - asking, testing, being wrong, correcting - was how a soul was actually formed. Your doubters stood inside a praying community. They questioned inside the rule of faith, and they were expected to bring the question to a teacher rather than carry it alone.

You ask what our response would be. It is this: we believe the one you cannot yet believe is the Logos, God's own Word, through whom all things were made, come in flesh to heal us from within. We believe he is the door, and that it stands open. We would not force you through it. We would stand at it with you, for as long as it took.

answer_text:
We received our practices, and we kept the receiving visible. Baptism, the bread and cup - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving - the scriptures read aloud were the tradition's general, unobjected practice. The rule of faith is the one our teachers named outright as the apostles' deposit, handed down.

What we can show is real. Our practice ran unbroken as far back as our own memory reached. We agreed with the other churches we were in communion with. And our rule of faith matched the apostolic writings we read. That shows how the receiving worked: not only through rites kept, but through souls formed, step by step, in a relationship that passed understanding on.

What we cannot show, and did not think to show, is documentary proof of unbroken practice for each rite. Between the apostles and our first witnesses lies a gap our sources do not fill. We will not pretend that gap away. What we held was the handing-on itself as visible fact: we received, we kept, we passed on. The proof we offered was coherence - with the other churches, with the apostolic writings, and with our own unbroken memory - not a paper trail for every gesture at the water or the table.
